title: Leveraging Social Media as a Thermometer to Gauge Patient and Caregiver Concerns: COVID-19 and Prostate Cancer
screen_reason: Mixed-methods study of posts by prostate cancer patients and caregivers to the Inspire Us TOO online community and to Reddit, December 2019 - April 2020. All 207 posts mentioning COVID, COVID-19 or coronavirus (191 Inspire, 16 Reddit) were coded manually by four trained coders using a codebook that included the presence of misinformation. Misinformation was present in 14 posts (7%), a share of items with a stated denominator, judged against factual accuracy (inaccurate COVID-19/influenza comparisons, false claims about masks and stay-at-home orders, misinformation about vaccines and treatments). CONTENT.

estimates.country: Predominantly USA (69% of posts), Canada (17%), other (6%), unknown (8%)
estimates.platform: Inspire Us TOO Prostate Cancer online support community and Reddit, pooled
estimates.measure_type: % of COVID-19-related posts by prostate cancer patients and caregivers that contained misinformation
estimates.denominator: 207 posts mentioning COVID, COVID-19 or coronavirus (191 to the Inspire Us TOO Prostate Cancer community and 16 from Reddit), drawn from 6,187 Inspire posts and 260 Reddit posts collected December 2019 - April 2020
estimates.definition: Coders recorded the presence of misinformation in the post; the misinformation topics reported were inaccurate comparisons between COVID-19 and influenza, false claims about public health strategies (masks, stay-at-home orders), and misinformation about COVID-19 vaccines and treatments (e.g. hydroxychloroquine, remdesivir)
estimates.misinfo_def: No formal definition given; the paper enumerates the types found: "Topics of misinformation included inaccurate comparisons between COVID-19 and influenza, false claims about public health strategies (eg, masks and stay-at-home orders), and misinformation about vaccines and treatments for COVID-19 (eg, hydroxychloroquine, remdesivir)."
estimates.source_quote: Misinformation was present in 7% of COVID-19–related posts.
estimates.page_loc: Abstract; main text p. 2 ('misinformation was present in 14 posts (7%)')
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Posts coded independently by four trained coders using a codebook created and refined by the study team, covering poster characteristics, prostate cancer characteristics, post topic and the presence of misinformation. No inter-rater reliability statistic is reported and the adjudication procedure for disagreements is not described. Study protocol approved by the NYU IRB.
estimates.moderator_quote: Manual qualitative analysis was performed for all posts to the Inspire Us TOO Prostate Cancer online support and discussion community and Reddit that mentioned COVID, COVID-19, or coronavirus. Posts were coded independently by four trained coders using a codebook created and refined by the study team.
estimates.notes: population_scope='other': the posters are prostate cancer patients and their partners/family members, not the general public and not professionals. country_norm='Multi-country' because the geography of the Inspire posters is enumerated (USA 143, Canada 35, Other 13, Unknown 16); the residual 'Other' category is unspecified, so 'Global' would also be defensible. Denominator is the COVID-mentioning subset (207), not all posts collected (6,447), because that is the set that was coded for misinformation. 14/207 = 6.8%, which the paper rounds to 7%; the verbatim 7% is used.

missed_or_uncertain: Nothing else in the paper is a misinformation share. Table 1 reports contributor demographics (median age 66, 52% male, 69% USA), disease stage, treatments, and main post topic (COVID-19 itself 37%, impact on cancer care 26%, impact on clinical trials 6% etc.) - all descriptors of the 207 coded posts, none of them veracity judgements. The LIWC/WordNet Affect linguistic ethnography results (more collective tone, increased concern with death, fewer emotion mentions in 2020) are word-category comparisons, not shares of misinformation. No per-platform breakdown of the 14 misinformation posts is given, so the Inspire and Reddit sets cannot be split.

rob.design: Mixed-methods observational study of two online communities. Frame: all anonymized public posts to the Inspire Us TOO Prostate Cancer community (>25,000 members) from December 2019 to April 2020 (6,187 posts) obtained under a data use agreement, plus 260 Reddit posts on prostate cancer over the same window; both compared to the same interval in 2019 (6,926 and 246 posts). Computational arm: LIWC and WordNet Affect linguistic ethnography comparing 2020 with 2019. Qualitative arm: all 207 posts mentioning COVID, COVID-19 or coronavirus coded independently by four trained coders against a study-team codebook. No inter-rater reliability reported; no description of how coder disagreements were resolved; the Reddit sampling procedure is not described. Authors note that people who post in online networks may not generalise to all prostate cancer patients and caregivers, and that many posts lacked demographic, stage and treatment detail. NYU IRB approved.
rob.item6_quote: The codebook categorized the characteristics of individuals generating posts (eg, patient, partners/family member, other), PCa characteristics (eg, any staging or treatment data presented), topic of the post (eg, COVID-19 itself, impact of COVID-19 on cancer treatment, impact of COVID-19 on clinical trials, etc.), and the presence of misinformation.
rob.item10_quote: A total of 191 posts to the Inspire PCa community and 16 posts from Reddit were specifically related to COVID-19 ... There was also discussion about COVID-19 itself, and misinformation was present in 14 posts (7%).
